title: Logging in the US
one_liner: US logging remains a fragmented, housing-linked timber supply industry, with 2025 revenue near $16.1 billion and output still below the 2021-2022 lumber-price boom.
overview: The industry cuts, skids, sorts and hauls timber from private, state and federal forests, with most volume tied to sawlogs for construction lumber and a smaller but important pulpwood and chip stream for paper, packaging, panels and energy. The 2022 baseline report captured the peak of the pandemic lumber cycle, when 2021 revenue reached $17.3 billion after a 17.3% surge. By 2025, public market summaries put US logging revenue around $16.1 billion, while Federal Reserve industrial production data show logging output at a 2025 index of 75.4, down from 80.4 in 2024 and 101.3 in 2022. The current market is mixed: weak housing starts and mill closures limit log demand, but trade restrictions, Canadian supply pressure, wildfire risk reduction and federal timber policy are supporting domestic supply attention.

baseline_2022.context: The 2022 file framed 2021 as a pandemic-price peak driven by a 34.0% sawmill lumber price increase and expected revenue to normalize toward $16.2 billion by 2026.

how_it_makes_money: Selling delivered sawlogs and bolts to sawmills for dimensional lumber, plywood, veneer and engineered wood products.
Selling pulpwood, chips and residues to pulp, paper, packaging and panel mills.
Providing contract harvesting, hauling, road-building and site-preparation services for timberland owners.
Capturing internal transfer value where vertically integrated timber REITs and forest-products companies harvest from owned timberlands for affiliated mills.
Selling specialty logs, biomass feedstock, seedlings or ancillary forest products in local markets.

cost_structure.labor: High-skilled equipment operators, truck drivers, supervisors and mechanics remain a major cost; BLS reported 2025 mean annual wages of $54,350 for logging equipment operators and $53,590 for heavy and tractor-trailer truck drivers in forestry and logging.
cost_structure.fuel_transport: Diesel, tires, maintenance, road access and haul distance are critical margin variables because logs are bulky and low value per unit weight.
cost_structure.equipment: Fellers, skidders, loaders, processors, chippers and trucks require heavy capital outlays and high maintenance spending.
cost_structure.stumpage_and_contracts: Operators either buy standing timber, pay stumpage, or work under harvesting contracts for timberland owners; stumpage pricing varies sharply by species, region and mill demand.
cost_structure.insurance_safety_compliance: Logging has elevated safety risk; BLS reported 67 fatalities in forestry and logging in 2024, making workers' compensation, liability coverage and training material costs.
cost_structure.profitability: Baseline 2021 profit margin was 5.0%; current margins are pressured by weak pulpwood demand and higher operating costs but helped where sawtimber prices and tariff-supported domestic demand improve realizations.

Rayonier Inc.
PotlatchDeltic Corporation
Sierra Pacific Industries
Green Diamond Resource Company
Hancock Natural Resource Group / Manulife Investment Management timberland clients
current_dynamics: Residential construction is the main swing factor: May 2026 housing starts were 1.177 million SAAR, 8.7% below May 2025, limiting near-term sawlog demand.

Supply-side pricing has firmed despite softer housing, with the June 2026 softwood lumber PPI at 286.523 and trade press reporting summer 2026 framing lumber prices near multiyear highs because of reduced imports, tariffs and mill curtailments.

Federal policy turned more pro-harvest in 2025 through Executive Order 14225 and USDA's $200 million active forest management investment, but GAO reported in June 2026 that Forest Service staffing cuts and legal challenges may constrain timber-sale execution.

Southern markets remain central because of plantation supply, sawmill investment and pulpwood demand, though USDA reported Southern pulpwood production fell to 52.1 million cords in 2024 from 52.9 million in 2023.
Canadian softwood duties and tariffs improve the relative position of domestic timber and sawmills but can also raise downstream lumber costs and create demand friction for builders.
whats_growing: Federal and state interest in active forest management, thinning and wildfire-risk reduction projects after the March 2025 timber executive order.
Domestic mill share where Canadian imports are constrained by 2025-2026 duties and tariffs.
Southern sawtimber exposure where new and upgraded sawmills need reliable pine log supply.
Data-enabled harvesting, cut-to-length systems, telematics and optimized trucking that reduce labor and fuel intensity.
Forest carbon, conservation easements and land-based solutions as supplemental income streams for timberland owners, even when they do not directly increase logging volume.
whats_shrinking: Logging output volume, with the Federal Reserve logging industrial production index falling from 101.3 in 2022 to 75.4 in 2025.
Employment intensity, as BLS's logging employment index fell to 84.593 in 2025 from 97.185 in 2021.
Pulpwood demand in regions hit by paper, pulp or panel mill closures; Rayonier reported weaker 2025 Atlantic-region pulpwood pricing tied partly to mill closures.
Pacific Northwest export-log exposure, pressured by weaker Asian demand, acreage dispositions and policy constraints.
Small independent contractor resilience, as high equipment costs, insurance, labor scarcity and volatile mill demand favor better-capitalized operators.
recent_developments: 2025-03-01: Executive Order 14225 directed USDA and Interior to accelerate domestic timber production and streamline forest-management approvals.
2025-03-01: A separate Section 232 order launched a national-security investigation into timber, lumber and derivative-product imports.
2025-05-29: USDA announced a $200 million investment for the Forest Service National Active Forest Management Strategy.
2025-08-08: Commerce finalized Canadian softwood lumber countervailing duty rates of 12.12% to 16.82%; amended all-others combined AD/CVD cash deposits later stood at 35.16%.
2026-06-04: GAO reported the Forest Service averaged about 90% of timber-sale targets in fiscal 2014-2023 and that 2025 staffing reductions could make expanded timber sales harder.
2026-07-15: FRED/BLS reported the June 2026 softwood lumber PPI at 286.523, above May 2026's 280.370.
outlook: Revenue is likely to remain volatile through 2026-2027. Higher tariffs and reduced Canadian supply can lift domestic log and lumber pricing, but weak housing starts, elevated mortgage rates, trucking costs, insurance costs and pulp mill closures cap volume growth. The most favorable operators are those near efficient Southern and Inland mills, with secure timber access, modern equipment, strong safety records and flexible sawtimber-versus-pulpwood merchandising. Federal timber initiatives could add supply over time, but permitting, lawsuits, staffing and mill capacity mean policy support is unlikely to translate into an immediate volume surge.
one_sentence: Logging companies harvest softwood and hardwood sawlogs, pulpwood and wood chips for sawmills, pulp mills, engineered-wood plants and biomass users, so revenue moves with lumber prices, housing starts, paper demand, mill capacity and access to harvestable timber.

title: Lotteries & Native American Casinos in the US
one_liner: State lotteries and tribal casinos remain a large, government-linked gambling market, with lottery ticket sales stable and tribal gaming still setting records after the pandemic rebound.
overview: This industry covers state and other general lotteries, Native American gaming facilities, video lottery and gambling machines, pari-mutuel wagering, bingo, charity games and card rooms, while excluding most commercial casino hotels. The 2022 baseline was dominated by traditional lotteries, which accounted for 68.6% of revenue, with Native American gaming facilities at 23.8%, other gaming at 5.0% and gambling machines at 2.6%. By 2025, the industry had moved from pandemic recovery into slower expansion: lottery sales remained above $113.3 billion in FY2024, while Indian gaming GGR reached a record $46.2 billion in FY2025.

key_stats.lottery_sales: FY2024 US lottery sales: over $113.3 billion
key_stats.tribal_gaming_ggr: FY2025 Indian gaming GGR: $46.2 billion, up 5.3% from FY2024
key_stats.tribal_operations: FY2025 Indian gaming data covered 545 gaming operations across 29 states
key_stats.commercial_gaming_context: CY2025 US commercial gaming GGR outside this IBIS category reached $78.72 billion, up 9.2%, increasing competition for discretionary gambling spend

how_it_makes_money: Lottery operators generate sales from instant tickets, draw games, multi-state jackpot games, keno and related products, with a large share returned as prizes and the balance funding state beneficiaries, retailer commissions and operating costs. Tribal casinos generate gross gaming revenue from slots, table games, bingo, poker, food and beverage, entertainment and resort amenities, with gaming revenue defined by NIGC as wagers minus winnings paid to players. Smaller segments earn revenue from video lottery terminals, pari-mutuel wagering, charitable bingo, card rooms and gambling-machine operations.
cost_structure: The largest cash outflow for lotteries is prize payouts, followed by transfers to state beneficiaries, retailer commissions, advertising, ticket systems, central gaming systems and administration. Tribal casino costs are more labor- and facility-intensive, including wages, benefits, gaming equipment, surveillance and compliance, food and beverage, utilities, maintenance, insurance and compact-related revenue sharing. The 2022 baseline profit margin was 13.5%, pressured by labor, reopening costs, gaming taxes and fixed facility expenses.

current_dynamics: The post-2020 rebound has largely normalized, but tribal gaming continues to outpace the mature lottery segment. FY2025 Indian gaming GGR rose 5.3% to $46.2 billion, while FY2024 US lottery sales remained over $113.3 billion. Competition is intensifying from regulated commercial casinos, online sports betting, iGaming, sweepstakes casinos, skill machines and sports-event prediction markets. Physical casinos benefit from tourism and local entertainment demand, while lotteries depend on convenience-store traffic, large jackpots, digital account funding and new instant-ticket price points.
whats_growing: Tribal casino GGR, low-denomination slot play, resort-style tribal properties, iLottery where legal, higher-priced instant tickets, multi-state jackpot games during large jackpot cycles, digital player accounts, loyalty programs and responsible-gaming technology are growing in 2025-2026.
whats_shrinking: Legacy pari-mutuel wagering, traditional horse-racing attendance, charitable bingo in many markets, smaller card rooms, low-jackpot draw-game momentum and some table-game economics are shrinking or under pressure in 2025-2026. Lottery sales growth is also slower than online gaming growth, making the lottery share of total gambling spend vulnerable over time.
recent_developments: 2025-07-31: NIGC announced FY2024 Indian gaming GGR of $43.9 billion, up 4.6% from FY2023.
2026-02-26: AGA reported CY2025 US commercial gaming GGR of $78.72 billion, up 9.2%, highlighting rising cross-sector competition.
2026-02-26: AGA reported CY2025 iGaming revenue of $10.74 billion, up 27.6%, showing the fastest-growing substitute for physical gaming and lottery products.
2026-07-16: AGA's May 2026 tracker reported traditional commercial casino revenue of $4.68 billion for May 2026, up 4.5% year over year.
2026-07-17: NIGC published its FY2025 GGR report; reported FY2025 Indian gaming GGR reached $46.2 billion, up 5.3% from FY2024.
outlook: The industry is expected to grow modestly through 2026 as tribal casinos continue to benefit from local entertainment demand, tourism, hotel amenities and slot revenue, while lotteries remain resilient but mature. Growth should be slower than online sports betting and iGaming, and margin pressure will persist from labor, compliance, marketing and facility costs. The most important upside is broader digital lottery adoption and continued tribal resort investment; the biggest risks are cannibalization from online gambling, affordability pressure on lower-income lottery customers, stricter responsible-gaming scrutiny and legal disputes over unregulated prediction-market and sweepstakes products.

title: Lubricant Oil Manufacturing in the US
one_liner: A mature petroleum-products manufacturing industry where synthetic oils, industrial demand and fleet age support volumes, while crude/base-oil prices drive revenue swings.
overview: Lubricant Oil Manufacturing in the US covers establishments that blend or compound refined petroleum into lubricating oils, greases, brake fluids, transmission fluids and oil-based additives. The 2022 IBISWorld baseline placed industry revenue at $25.886 billion after 5.8% growth in 2022, with automotive lubricants at 46.4% of 2022 revenue and industrial lubricants at 49.0%. Current market evidence points to a larger demand-side US lubricants market than the manufacturing-only baseline: MarketsandMarkets estimated the US lubricants market at $37.715 billion in 2025, while Grand View Research estimated $41.71 billion in 2024 and $42.28 billion in 2025. The industry remains mature, fragmented below the integrated oil majors, and highly exposed to petroleum feedstock prices, but premium synthetics, lower-viscosity engine oils, industrial process oils, metalworking fluids and reliability-focused maintenance products are improving mix.

how_it_makes_money: Manufacturers buy base oils, refined petroleum streams, additive packages, packaging and blending services, then sell finished lubricants and greases through petroleum wholesalers, chemical distributors, automotive retail chains, oil-change operators, fleet accounts, OEM channels and direct industrial sales. Revenue is earned from passenger-car motor oils, heavy-duty diesel engine oils, transmission and brake fluids, hydraulic fluids, gear oils, process oils, metalworking fluids, greases and specialty products. Higher margins come from synthetic blends, full synthetics, OEM-approved formulations, private-label programs, specialty industrial fluids, extended-drain products and technical services such as oil analysis.
cost_structure: The 2022 baseline shows profit at 6.5% of revenue and wages at $1.455 billion, or about 5.6% of 2022 revenue. Purchases are the dominant cost category because base oil, additives, refined petroleum inputs, containers and freight move with crude and refinery economics; EIA estimated Brent crude at $69 per barrel in 2025 and $82 per barrel in 2026. Other material costs include additive chemistry, packaging resin, drums, bottles, labels and pallets. Operating costs include energy for blending and heating, quality testing, compliance, environmental controls, R&D, depreciation on blending and storage assets, warehousing and outbound logistics. Pricing power is strongest in branded synthetics and technical industrial products, and weakest in commodity/private-label conventional oils.

current_dynamics: The industry is balancing better unit demand in industrial and maintenance channels against pressure from longer oil-change intervals, EV adoption and volatile petroleum inputs. Industrial demand improved in 2026: the Federal Reserve reported total industrial production up 1.1% year over year in June 2026 and manufacturing output rising at a 4.7% annual rate in Q2 2026. Automotive maintenance remains resilient because S&P Global Mobility put the average US light-vehicle age at 12.8 years in 2025 and vehicles in operation at 289 million in 2025. At the same time, EVs reduce engine-oil demand per vehicle, although the EV share fell from 7.8% in full-year 2025 to 5.8% in Q1 2026 after US purchase incentives ended. Input prices are still a swing factor: BLS/FRED showed the lubricating oil and grease manufacturing PPI at 735.435 in June 2026, up from 653.461 in March 2026. Refinery and base-oil supply risk also matters after EIA reported about 400,000 barrels per day of US operable refinery-capacity reductions from 2025 closures.
whats_growing: Full synthetic and synthetic-blend motor oils, GF-7/API SQ passenger-car formulations licensed from March 31, 2025, lower-viscosity oils for fuel economy, heavy-duty fleet lubricants, industrial process oils, hydraulic fluids, metalworking fluids, high-performance greases, oil-analysis services, private-label programs and specialty fluids for hybrids, EV drivetrains, thermal management and advanced manufacturing equipment.
whats_shrinking: Conventional passenger-car motor oil is losing share as extended-drain synthetics stretch replacement intervals. Older GF-6/API SP inventory is being phased down after the March 31, 2025 GF-7/API SQ launch and the March 31, 2026 GF-6 last-license transition cited by Valvoline. Light-vehicle engine-oil volume faces long-term erosion from battery-electric vehicles, even though 2026 EV penetration softened. West Coast refinery closures are reducing regional supply flexibility, and small independent blenders remain exposed to feedstock, packaging and compliance-cost volatility.
recent_developments: 2025-03-31: API SQ / ILSAC GF-7 passenger-car motor oil licensing began, raising fuel-economy, deposit, wear and LSPI requirements.
2025-05-21: S&P Global Mobility reported US light-vehicle average age rose to 12.8 years in 2025 and vehicles in operation reached 289 million.
2025-10-01: Phillips 66 said it was idling its Los Angeles refinery, with final crude processing expected around October 16, 2025.
2026-01-13: Cox Automotive said 2025 US EV sales share was 7.8%, down from 8.1% in 2024, with Q4 2025 EV sales down 46% from Q3 2025.
2026-07-17: The Federal Reserve reported June 2026 industrial production up 1.1% year over year and Q2 2026 manufacturing output up at a 4.7% annual rate.
2026-07-15: BLS/FRED reported the petroleum lubricating oil and grease manufacturing PPI at 735.435 for June 2026.
outlook: The outlook is modestly positive in value terms but mixed in volume terms. Demand should be supported by the 12.8-year 2025 vehicle age, 289 million vehicles in operation in 2025, high-15-million to low-16-million 2026 new-vehicle sales conditions, and a 2026 rebound in manufacturing output. Premium synthetics and industrial fluids should lift average selling prices and margins, while EVs, longer drain intervals and maturing vehicle oil demand cap long-run volume. Input-price uncertainty remains central: EIA’s July 2026 STEO placed Brent at $82 per barrel in 2026 after $69 per barrel in 2025, and the June 2026 lubricant PPI spike shows that formulators may still face margin compression when base-oil and additive costs rise faster than contracts can reset. A reasonable current framing is low-single-digit annual market growth through 2030, with higher growth in specialty industrial and synthetic products and flat-to-declining conventional automotive oils.
one_sentence: US lubricant oil manufacturers blend and compound refined petroleum, synthetic base stocks, additives and greases for automotive, industrial, fleet, marine and machinery users, with 2025-2026 performance shaped by crude-price volatility, newer engine-oil standards, aging vehicles, EV adoption and industrial production.

title: Lumber & Building Material Stores in the US
one_liner: Lumberyards and building-material dealers are a contractor-led retail channel caught between weak single-family construction, resilient repair-and-remodel demand, volatile lumber costs and accelerating consolidation.
overview: This industry consists of stores and dealers, including lumberyards, that retail new building materials such as lumber, hardwood, stone, brick, cabinets, floor coverings, roofing materials, plumbing and electrical goods, doors and windows. It excludes home improvement centers, paint and wallpaper specialty stores, and hardware stores. Demand is tied most directly to residential construction, repair-and-remodel work and contractor activity, while pricing is heavily influenced by lumber and other building-product commodity cycles. The 2022 IBISWorld baseline described a fragmented, mature industry with low concentration, strong contractor exposure and rising competition from big-box home improvement retailers. Current 2025-2026 conditions are more mixed: nominal industry revenue remains above the 2021 pandemic-boom baseline, but single-family housing starts fell in 2025, repair-and-remodel growth is slowing into 2026, and tariffs and duties on Canadian softwood lumber have lifted supply-cost risk.

how_it_makes_money: Stores earn revenue by selling lumber, engineered wood, trusses, millwork, windows, doors, roofing, siding, flooring, cabinets, plumbing and electrical supplies, fasteners, tools and other building materials. The core customer is the professional contractor or builder purchasing for new construction, remodeling, maintenance and repair jobs, while do-it-yourself consumers remain a secondary channel. Dealers compete on inventory availability, jobsite delivery, credit terms, estimating support, installed sales, specialty product knowledge and local relationships rather than only shelf price.

cost_structure.purchases: In 2025-2026, merchandise purchases remain the dominant cost because dealers resell lumber, panels, millwork, cabinets, roofing, plumbing and electrical supplies; cost risk is elevated by lumber volatility and tariffs on wood products.
cost_structure.labor: The 2022 baseline showed $17.8 billion of wages in 2021, equal to about 12.1% of 2021 revenue; current labor costs remain pressured by warehouse, driver, sales and skilled installed-services staffing needs.
cost_structure.profit: The 2022 baseline profit margin was 5.4% in 2021; 2025-2026 margins are pressured by weaker starts, competitive pricing and uneven pass-through of lumber and tariff costs.
cost_structure.freight_and_delivery: 2025-2026 dealers rely on truck fleets, jobsite delivery and branch logistics, making fuel, insurance, driver availability and route density important operating costs.
cost_structure.rent_utilities_and_property: Branch yards, showrooms, warehouses and outdoor storage create recurring occupancy and utility costs, with higher burdens in dense construction markets.
cost_structure.technology: 2025-2026 spending is shifting toward e-commerce portals, contractor account tools, inventory systems, pricing engines, delivery scheduling and ERP integration.

current_dynamics: The demand backdrop in 2025-2026 is split. New single-family construction is soft because mortgage rates, affordability and builder caution reduced starts, directly hurting framing lumber, trusses, panels, windows and millwork volumes. Repair-and-remodel demand is still large because homeowners with low-rate mortgages are staying put and improving existing homes, but Harvard JCHS expects growth to slow through 2026. Supply costs are again a strategic issue: Canadian softwood lumber duties and 2025 Section 232 wood-product tariffs increased landed costs and supported higher lumber prices in 2026, even as housing activity cooled. The channel is also consolidating as national and regional players use acquisitions, manufacturing capabilities, installed sales and pro-account technology to defend share against Home Depot, Lowe's and other big-box competitors.
whats_growing: Installed sales, component manufacturing, trusses, wall panels, millwork and value-added services that deepen contractor relationships in 2025-2026.
Repair, maintenance and aging-in-place remodeling tied to a large existing-home base, with owner-occupied improvement and repair spending projected at $518 billion by year-end 2026.
Digital contractor portals, online account history, quote tools, inventory visibility and delivery scheduling in 2025-2026.
Specialty building products, including windows, doors, millwork, engineered components, roofing, siding and cabinetry, as dealers seek margin beyond commodity lumber.
Green and code-compliant products, including certified lumber, energy-efficient windows, lower-toxicity materials and resilient building products in 2025-2026.
whats_shrinking: Single-family new-construction demand, with US single-family starts down 6.9% in 2025 from 2024.
Commodity-sensitive lumber volumes at pro dealers when builders delay starts and when high prices reduce project affordability in 2025-2026.
Small independent dealer share in markets where larger chains and acquisition platforms gain purchasing scale, branch density and technology budgets.
DIY-oriented traffic at specialty lumberyards as big-box home improvement stores continue to capture convenience-driven consumers in 2025-2026.
Remodeling growth momentum, with Harvard JCHS projecting growth easing to 1.6% by late 2026.
recent_developments: 2025-06: IBISWorld's June 2025 industry report estimated Lumber & Building Material Stores revenue at $152.8 billion after a 3.4% CAGR over 2020-2025.
2025-08: The US Commerce Department finalized Canadian softwood lumber countervailing duty rates ranging from 12.12% to 16.82%.
2025-10: The United States imposed a 10% Section 232 global tariff on timber and softwood lumber effective October 14, 2025.

2026-07: Harvard JCHS said remodeling spending was poised for further slowdown through mid-2027 after earlier 2026 projections showed growth easing to 1.6% by late 2026.
2026-08: Lumber prices reached a reported $535 per thousand board feet, up 23% year over year, despite a weak housing market.
outlook: The 2026 outlook is cautious but not recessionary for the channel. Revenue is likely to remain supported by price inflation, repair-and-remodel spending and contractor demand for specialty products, but unit volume is constrained by weak single-family starts and affordability pressure. Dealers with scale, inventory discipline, value-added manufacturing, installed services and digital contractor tools should outperform smaller commodity-heavy yards. Tariffs and duties can lift nominal sales if costs are passed through, but they also raise project costs and can suppress demand. A stronger recovery likely depends on lower mortgage rates, improved builder confidence and a turn in single-family permits and starts.

title: Lumber Wholesaling in the US
one_liner: A construction-supply distribution industry that reset from 2022 lumber-price highs but remains exposed to housing starts, renovation demand, tariffs and volatile wood-product costs.
overview: The industry sits between sawmills, wood-products manufacturers and the construction channel. Baseline 2022 revenue was inflated by pandemic-era shortages and lumber prices, while 2023-2025 output normalized as housing activity cooled and commodity prices deflated. By 2026, the demand side remains constrained by mortgage rates and uneven housing starts, but supply-side pressures have reappeared as Canadian duties, 2025 Section 232 lumber tariffs and mill curtailments push lumber prices higher. Operators with scale, branch density, inventory discipline and value-added services are better positioned than commodity-only wholesalers.

baseline_2022.market_size: 2022: $200.8 billion IBISWorld industry revenue in 2022 dollars
baseline_2022.product_mix: 2022: lumber and boards 36.6%, plywood and panels 23.3%, wood millwork 20.1%, other products 20.0%

how_it_makes_money: Wholesalers earn gross margin by sourcing wood and millwork products in bulk, holding inventory near construction markets, extending credit, breaking bulk, coordinating delivery and offering jobsite logistics or cut-to-order/value-added services. Revenue is concentrated in lumber and boards, plywood and panels, wood millwork, doors, windows, frames and related construction products sold to home builders, commercial contractors, carpenters, hardware stores and building-material retailers.
cost_structure: Cost of goods is the dominant expense because lumber, panels and millwork are commodity-heavy inputs. Public distributor benchmarks show 2025 gross margins of 15.3% at BlueLinx and 15.1% in Boise Cascade Building Materials Distribution, implying 2025 product and operating costs near 85% of sales before SG&A. Other major costs include wages for warehouse, sales and delivery staff, freight and fuel, rent and yard costs, working-capital financing, shrinkage, bad debt and IT/inventory systems. Baseline IBISWorld profit margin was 4.5% in 2022, with margins expected to compress when lumber prices deflate or inventory is bought ahead of price declines.
major_players: Builders FirstSource: 2025 net sales of $15.2 billion, including $3.9 billion from lumber and lumber sheet goods
Boise Cascade Building Materials Distribution: 2025 segment sales of $5.9 billion
BlueLinx: 2025 net sales of $3.0 billion across specialty and structural building products
84 Lumber: 2025 Forbes Top Private Companies rank No. 98 and described itself as the largest privately held US building-materials supplier
ABC Supply: large building-products distributor with selective exposure to lumber, millwork and adjacent exterior products
current_dynamics: The industry is no longer riding the extreme 2021-2022 price boom, but 2026 conditions are not simply weak demand. June 2026 starts and permits show a mixed construction pipeline, while May 2026 wholesale sales remain sizable at $18.2 billion. Tariffs and duties on Canadian softwood lumber, reduced Canadian imports and North American mill curtailments have tightened supply and lifted prices even as housing affordability weighs on builders and remodelers.
whats_growing: Value-added and specialty categories are gaining share relative to pure commodity lumber. In 2025, BlueLinx specialty-products sales rose 0.3% to $2.1 billion while structural products fell 0.6%; Boise Cascade reported 2025 BMD mix of 45.2% general line and 19.8% engineered wood products. Engineered wood, millwork, doors, windows, outdoor living, specialty panels, digital inventory visibility and project logistics are stronger growth lanes than undifferentiated framing lumber.
whats_shrinking: Commodity-sensitive revenue tied to lumber and panels has contracted from 2022 highs as prices normalized and builders operated in a below-normal starts environment. Builders FirstSource reported 2025 net sales down 7.4%, with lumber and lumber sheet goods down 9.2%; BlueLinx reported 2025 structural-products sales down 0.6% and lower gross profit. Smaller, price-taking wholesalers remain pressured by consolidation, freight costs, financing costs and inventory-price risk.
recent_developments: 2025-03-07: NAHB said proposed Canada and Mexico tariffs could raise imported construction-material costs by more than $3.0 billion and add $7,500-$10,000 to an average new single-family home based on member reports.
2025-08-08: The US Commerce Department finalized Canadian softwood-lumber countervailing duty rates of 12.12%-16.82% for the sixth administrative review.
2025-09-30: NAHB reported a new 10% Section 232 tariff on timber and lumber imports effective October 14, 2025, adding to Canadian softwood-lumber duties.
2025-10-31: BlueLinx acquired Disdero Lumber, expanding specialty building-products distribution in the Pacific Northwest.
2026-06-03: BLS/FRED updated 2025 sectoral output for NAICS 4233 to $188.1 billion, up 0.2% from 2024 but down from $223.7 billion in 2022.
2026-08-06: WSJ reported lumber prices at a four-year high, with the Random Lengths Framing Lumber Composite at $535 per thousand board feet and up 23% year over year.
outlook: The 2026-2028 outlook is mixed. Revenue should benefit if supply constraints and tariffs keep lumber prices elevated, but volume growth depends on lower mortgage rates, improved housing affordability and a recovery in single-family starts. Margins should remain volatile because wholesalers can gain on rising inventory values but lose quickly when commodity prices reverse. Scale operators are likely to keep acquiring regional distributors, investing in logistics and shifting toward engineered wood, millwork and specialty products to reduce exposure to commodity lumber cycles.

Specialty and engineered wood products outperform structural lumber
Distributor consolidation favors scale and branch density
